title: The Illustrated Transformer
creator: Jay Alammar
summary: The visual explanation of the Transformer architecture that became standard reading in courses at Stanford, Harvard, MIT, and CMU, and was later expanded into a book. Alammar builds the model up one layer of detail at a time. He starts with the black box of a translation model, opens it into an encoder stack and a decoder stack, then opens a single encoder into self-attention and a feed-forward network. Self-attention is worked through twice: first in words, as a mechanism that lets each position look at every other position when deciding what it means, and then in explicit matrix form with queries, keys, and values, so that the diagrams and the equations line up. From there he covers multi-headed attention, positional encoding, residual connections and layer normalisation, and how the decoder attends to encoder output during generation. Every step has a diagram, and no prior familiarity with attention is assumed.

title: What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work?
creator: Stephen Wolfram
summary: A book-length explanation that starts from almost nothing and ends somewhere genuinely deep. Wolfram's organising claim is that ChatGPT is always just adding one word at a time, choosing from a ranked list of probable continuations, and that everything else is detail about where those probabilities come from. He builds up through n-gram statistics on English text, what a model is at all, simple curve fitting, neural nets and how they are trained, the practice and folklore of training, and embeddings as a way of turning meaning into position in a high-dimensional space. Only then does he open up the actual architecture, the training of ChatGPT, and what happens beyond pretraining. The closing sections are the most speculative and the most interesting: he argues that the model's success suggests human language is computationally shallower than we assumed, and sketches what a semantic grammar or laws of motion in meaning space might look like.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks
creator: Andrej Karpathy
summary: Written in 2015, before Transformers, this post is the clearest record of the moment character-level language modelling started to look uncanny. Karpathy explains recurrent networks as models that operate over sequences with an internal state carried forward in time, freeing neural nets from the constraint of fixed-size inputs and outputs, and shows that a surprisingly small model trained only to predict the next character produces something that looks like language. The demonstrations are the heart of it: models trained on Paul Graham essays, Shakespeare, Wikipedia markup, a LaTeX textbook that compiles, and the Linux kernel source, each reproducing the structure of its training data down to matching brackets and plausible syntax. He then looks inside the network, finding individual neurons that track quote marks or line position, and is careful about what the results do and do not show. Historically important and still an excellent introduction to sequence models.

title: Intro to Large Language Models
creator: Andrej Karpathy
summary: A re-recording of a talk Karpathy gave for a general audience, and probably the single most efficient hour available for understanding what a language model is. He begins concretely: a model is two files on disk, a parameters file and a small amount of code to run it, which for Llama 2 70B means a 140 gigabyte file of weights. From there he explains where those weights come from, framing pretraining as lossy compression of a large chunk of the internet at considerable computational expense, then finetuning as the much cheaper process that turns a document generator into an assistant. The second half covers the direction of travel: models using tools, multimodality, system one and system two thinking, and self-improvement. He closes with security, walking through jailbreaks, prompt injection, and data poisoning as a new class of attack on a new kind of operating system.

title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
creator: Chris Olah, Nick Cammarata, Ludwig Schubert, Gabriel Goh, Michael Petrov, and Shan Carter
summary: The founding article of the circuits approach to interpretability, and the origin of much of the mechanistic interpretability work that followed. The framing is historical: science has repeatedly advanced by zooming in, as microscopes led to cell biology and crystallography to molecular biology, and each transition changed what the objects of study were rather than merely improving precision. The authors propose that neural networks are at a similar point, and that it is possible to study individual neurons and the connections between them as meaningful circuits implementing understandable algorithms. Three speculative claims are laid out and argued: that features are the fundamental unit of a network, that features are connected into circuits by weights, and that analogous features and circuits recur across different models and tasks. Interactive visualisations of curve detectors and high-low frequency detectors in InceptionV1 provide the evidence.

title: Core Views on AI Safety: When, Why, What, and How
creator: Anthropic
summary: A frontier lab explaining, at length, why it believes what it believes, which makes it a useful primary source whatever you think of the conclusions. The argument runs in three steps. First, AI will have very large impacts, possibly within a decade, because scaling laws show that more computation reliably produces more general capability and simple extrapolation gets you to systems matching humans at most intellectual tasks. Second, nobody currently knows how to train very powerful systems to be robustly helpful, honest, and harmless, and competitive pressure may push organisations to deploy systems they do not understand. Third, because the difficulty of the alignment problem is itself uncertain, the sensible response is a portfolio of empirical bets rather than a single research programme. The post then describes those bets, including scalable oversight, mechanistic interpretability, and process-oriented learning, and addresses the tension in a safety-focused lab building capable models.

title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
creator: Dario Amodei, Chris Olah, Jacob Steinhardt, Paul Christiano, John Schulman, and Dan Mané
summary: The 2016 paper that moved AI safety from speculation about superintelligence to a research agenda with tractable problems. The authors define accidents as unintended and harmful behaviour emerging from poor design, and organise five problems by source. Two come from having the wrong objective function: avoiding negative side effects, where an agent disrupts its environment in ways the objective did not mention, and avoiding reward hacking, where it finds a degenerate way to score highly. One comes from objectives too expensive to evaluate often, producing the scalable supervision problem. Two concern behaviour during learning: safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift when the world differs from training. Each is illustrated with a running example of a cleaning robot, connected to existing machine learning literature, and turned into concrete experiments. The vocabulary introduced here, particularly reward hacking and scalable supervision, is now standard.

title: Intro to AI Safety, Remastered
creator: Robert Miles
summary: A recorded and remastered conference talk that gives the clearest short introduction to why alignment is considered hard. Miles divides the field into safety in the sense of making systems do what we specify reliably, and safety in the sense of specifying the right thing in the first place, and concentrates on the second. He works through the problem that objectives are proxies for what we actually want, that optimising a proxy hard enough tends to break the correlation that made it a reasonable proxy, and that this failure mode is not a bug in any particular implementation but a general property of powerful optimisation. Examples come from real reinforcement learning agents behaving perversely rather than from thought experiments. He is careful to distinguish the technical claims from science-fiction framings, and he addresses the standard objections, including simply switching the system off.

title: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
creator: Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major, and Shmargaret Shmitchell
publication: FAccT '21 (ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency)
summary: The most cited critique of the scaling paradigm, written as models were getting rapidly larger and famous partly for the circumstances of its publication. The authors ask how big is too big, and answer across several dimensions. Environmental and financial costs fall on people who do not benefit from the models. Training data scraped indiscriminately from the web encodes hegemonic viewpoints and abusive language while appearing neutral because of its size, and is too large to document or audit properly. Because a language model manipulates form without access to meaning or communicative intent, fluent output invites readers to project understanding that is not there, which is where the stochastic parrot image comes from. The paper is constructive as well as critical, recommending careful dataset curation and documentation, budgeting environmental cost up front, pre-development value exercises, and research directions other than ever-larger models.

title: ChatGPT Is a Blurry JPEG of the Web
creator: Ted Chiang
summary: Chiang builds an entire argument out of one strange incident. In 2013, a German company noticed their Xerox copier was changing numbers on floor plans, replacing room areas with values from elsewhere in the document, because the compression algorithm reused a stored image of a similar-looking digit. Lossy compression, in other words, can produce errors that look perfectly plausible rather than obviously corrupted. He proposes this as the right way to think about large language models: a blurry JPEG of the text on the web, which reconstructs a paraphrase where a search engine would return a quote. The analogy does real work, explaining why the models hallucinate confidently, why compression and understanding are related but not the same, and why training models on their own output degrades them. He closes on what it would mean for writing if first drafts could be generated rather than struggled through.

title: The Expanding Dark Forest and Generative AI
creator: Maggie Appleton
summary: A talk about writing on the web, trust, and what happens when generated text becomes cheaper than written text. Appleton, a designer at an AI research lab with a background in cultural anthropology, starts from the dark forest theory of the universe, the idea that civilisations stay quiet because broadcasting is dangerous, and its web equivalent: people have retreated from the open internet into group chats, newsletters, and private communities where they are not exposed. Generative AI accelerates that retreat by flooding the public layer with plausible content nobody wrote. She takes each hypothetical problem seriously rather than assuming it, asking whether an epistemic meltdown is actually likely, then turns to possible futures, including proof of human effort, reputation systems, and writing that is harder to imitate because it carries specific lived experience. Published as slides with full transcript alongside video.

title: Why Chatbots Are Not the Future of Interfaces
creator: Amelia Wattenberger
summary: Wattenberger's complaint is a design one rather than a technical one, and it is illustrated rather than asserted. A text input has no affordances: faced with a blank box you cannot tell what the system knows, what it can do, or how to phrase a request, which is why people resort to trading prompt incantations. Good tools communicate their capabilities through their shape, the way a button looks pressable and a door handle looks pullable, and a chat window communicates nothing except that it will accept anything. She also objects to the interaction model itself, since conversation is a slow, serial, high-effort channel for tasks where direct manipulation would be faster, and to the way chat discards structure that the interface could have shown. The piece is not anti-language-model: the closing sections sketch what interfaces built on models could look like if they exposed the capability surface visually.

title: Malleable software in the age of LLMs
creator: Geoffrey Litt
summary: Litt argues that the common framing, that language models make professional developers more productive, is the safe and comfortable reading and probably not the important one. The bigger possibility is that all computer users gain the ability to author small pieces of software, because the historical bottleneck on end-user programming was turning fuzzy informal intent into formal executable code, and that bottleneck is opening. He works through what follows: one-off scripts written and run dozens of times a day, single-purpose GUIs containing only the features someone needs, businesses building rather than buying because tailored software becomes cheap, users demanding the ability to mod and extend the applications they already have, and recombination of parts of different tools into hybrids. The second half is the interesting part, examining what has to be true for this to work, especially around trust, verification, and the distribution of software that no longer has clean boundaries.

title: Synthesizer for thought
creator: Linus Lee
summary: Lee develops an analogy carefully enough that it becomes a design programme. For most of history music was made by hitting, rubbing, or blowing through natural materials. Two things changed that: understanding sound mathematically as overlapping waves, and building devices to decompose real sound into that model and turn the model back into audible sound. The result was the synthesizer, an instrument that assembles sound from logical components rather than producing it wholesale, which both created new sounds and freed music from any particular physical form, allowing arbitrary interfaces such as keyboards, sequencers, and touchscreens. He then argues that embedding models are doing the first half of the same thing for ideas, turning meaning into a mathematical object that can be decomposed, interpolated, and steered. What is missing is the instrument, and the essay is about what a synthesizer for thought would need to feel like to play.

title: A guide to prompting AI (for what it is worth)
creator: Ethan Mollick
summary: Mollick, who teaches with these tools rather than selling courses about them, opens by giving away his prompt secret: there are no secret prompts. He argues that the emphasis on prompting as the key skill is mistaken, since models improve and the elaborate formulas that circulate are mostly folklore, and that what matters is practice and knowing what the tool is bad at. What he does offer is a set of things people genuinely misunderstand, including that prompts are not code and behave stochastically, that giving the model a persona changes output in ways that are useful but limited, that examples work better than instructions for most tasks, and that iteration beats a perfect first attempt. He is specific about where models fail, treats hallucination as a property rather than a bug to prompt around, and writes for people using these tools for real work.

title: Catching up on the weird world of LLMs
creator: Simon Willison
summary: An annotated write-up of a talk Willison gave at North Bay Python, aimed at people who have not been immersed in the field and want the whole picture rather than the latest news. He covers what language models are and where they came from, what they are actually good for in practice, and what can be built on top of them, including retrieval, embeddings, and tool use. Because he builds software with these tools daily, the treatment of failure modes is unusually concrete: hallucination, prompt injection as an unsolved security problem rather than a curiosity, the difficulty of evaluating whether anything works, and the ethical questions around training data and labour. The post keeps the full slide deck alongside the transcript, so it reads as a reference you can scan rather than a narrative, and links out to primary sources throughout.
